report.markdown:
# Training plan: 14-month rescue border collie mix, South Bay

Three answers, in the order you asked for them.

---

## 1. Hire or DIY?

**Hybrid, weighted toward DIY.** Do the daily work yourself and buy a small amount of professional help up front — the $595 reactive-dog class, or two or three private sessions. Do not buy a big package yet.

**Why the daily work has to be yours.** Reactivity is treated by desensitisation and counter-conditioning in short, frequent sessions on real walks. You are the one holding the leash every evening. The $4,200 "trainer works your dog for you" option is the worst value for this specific problem.

**Why buy some help anyway:**

- **You need the right diagnosis, and it changes the plan.** A fearful dog is reactive because it feels trapped — the leash blocks its flight response and forces a fight display, and its goal is to make the other dog go *away*. Frustration reactivity is the opposite: he desperately wants to greet and can't. A hard-pulling collie mix is often frustration, but guessing wrong sends you down the wrong road for weeks. One good session settles it.
- **14 months is peak adolescence.** Hormones and maturation are a large part of why this shows up now, and every outburst is a rehearsal that makes it stickier.
- **A reactive-dog class gives you what you cannot manufacture alone:** controlled trigger dogs at a distance *you* choose. On a public street you get no say over how close the other dog comes.
- **He's a border collie mix.** High drive, high intelligence, and more likely than average to need a real mental outlet alongside the training.

**When to stop DIY-ing and escalate.** Mild-to-moderate reactivity is manageable by a committed owner. The bright lines that mean get help now: a bite history, escaping the harness, or redirected aggression — snapping at you when frustrated on leash.

**Non-negotiables on who you hire.** Force-free only. Look for CPDT-KA, KPA-CTP, CBCC-KA, IAABC, or CTC credentials. Avoid board-and-train and anything using e-collars or prong collars for reactivity — they suppress the outward behaviour without changing the underlying emotion.

---

## 2. Local options with real prices

All figures taken from each provider's own site, August 2026.

| | D For Dogz | In Tune Dog Training | HSSV (Milpitas) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Format** | Group class + private | Private, in your home | Group only |
| **Headline price** | **$595** — 9 sessions / 5 wks | **$195–$325** consult, then **$130–$215** per session | **$200** — 6 sessions |
| **Realistic total** | $595 | ~$845–$1,400 for a 6-session block | $200, less adopter discount |
| **Evenings / weekends** | Yes — Sat 9:30–10:30am + Wed 6:30–7:15pm Zoom | Weekends "upon request" — must confirm | Varies by class; same slot for 6 wks |
| **Reactivity-specific** | Yes, dedicated leash-reactive class | Yes | No — general manners only |
| **Contact** | 650-538-3011 | Nancy@Intunedogtraining.com | DogTraining@hssv.org |

### D For Dogz — best fit, and where I'd start
The **Leash Reactive Dog Foundations** class is **$595 for 9 sessions over 5 weeks**: in person Saturdays 9:30–10:30am, plus a live Zoom Q&A Wednesdays 6:30–7:15pm. The first two in-person sessions are people-only, and the last session is a guided neighbourhood walk. Requirements: current vaccinations, no history of aggressive bites toward humans. Classes are held at rotating real-world locations, which is good for generalising skills but means you should confirm where they actually meet.

Their private options, for reference: **Private Coaching $2,400 / 6 weeks** (weekly sessions on your own neighbourhood walks), **Day Training $4,200 / 6 weeks** (trainer works the dog twice weekly, you join every third session). There's a **free 15-minute discovery call** before you commit — take it.

### In Tune Dog Training — best private option
Nancy Le, San Jose, Fear Free certified, reward-based, in-home. **Initial consultation $195–$325**, which buys two 60-minute sessions (discovery, then plan review). **Follow-ups $130–$215 each.** She recommends starting with 6 sessions about twice a month. So a realistic first block is roughly **$845 at the low end, ~$1,400 at the top**.

Two things that matter: there's **tiered pricing for households under $115K/year**, and her service area is a **15-mile radius of Cambrian in San Jose** — covering Campbell, Sunnyvale, Cupertino, Santa Clara, Mountain View, Los Gatos, Milpitas and Los Altos. Weekend appointments are possible but explicitly "upon request," so that's the question to lead with.

### HSSV — the budget fallback
**$200 for six sessions** of Beginning Manners, and **adopters get a discount** — worth chasing since he's a rescue. Two real limitations: they offer **no private training or behaviour consults** to the general public, and they ask you to email first describing the behaviour so they can judge whether a reactive dog suits their group setting. Their free Reactive Dog Training Guide PDF is worth downloading regardless.

### Ruled out: Stacy's Wag'N'Train
Widely rated the top reactivity trainer in San Jose, CPDT-KA, and reasonably priced — $190 evaluation, $800 for a 4-pack, $1,500 for a behaviour-modification 6-pack. **Excluded purely on scheduling:** her site states private lessons are weekdays, daytime only, and she books 2–3 weeks out. Noting her in case your availability ever changes.

---

## 3. The four-week plan

Full detail is in the week-by-week subtasks. Structure:

**Week 0 (this weekend) — kit and rules.** ~$95–$165. Front-clip harness (the single biggest immediate change for a hard puller), 6ft fixed leash, 15–30ft long line, waist treat pouch, high-value soft treats he never otherwise gets. Scout one quiet route and one where dogs appear at a distance you control. Learn the emergency U-turn before you need it.

**Week 1 — measure, don't fix.** Loose-leash work only in boring places: stop dead when the leash tightens, move again on slack, feed at your leg. Separately, sit somewhere and just *observe* — at what distance does he notice, stare, then bark? That barking distance minus a margin is his **threshold**, typically 50–100 feet to start. Write the number down. Plus 2–3 long-line sniffing walks.

**Week 2 — Engage-Disengage, Level 1.** At threshold distance, let him notice a dog on his own; the moment he looks, mark; when he turns back to you, feed. The bar is **3–5 successful reps in a row at the same distance**. Sessions are **1–5 minutes**, then stop. Stop early on lip-licking, yawning or scratching.

**Week 3 — Level 2, and close the gap.** Now wait 1–5 seconds for him to look away *on his own*, and mark that. Fixating past 5 seconds means drop back to Level 1. After 3–5 good reps, move **1–5 steps** closer — that's the whole increment. Expect a bad day; that's normal.

**Week 4 — generalise, then assess.** Run the same game in 3–4 different locations, because skills that work in one spot collapse in a new one. Then review honestly: is the threshold number smaller? Fewer outbursts than week 1? Escalate to a pro if the distance hasn't shrunk at all, if he's worse, if you see redirected aggression, or if you're dreading walks.

**The one rule that governs all four weeks:** if he won't take a treat, he is over threshold and you are too close. That's your best real-time gauge, and it's free.

**Set the right target.** The realistic goal is a dog who can walk calmly past other dogs — not a dog park dog. Meaningful change in leash reactivity is measured in months, not weeks. Four good weeks means the method is right, not that you're done.

---

## What to do next

1. **Call D For Dogz on 650-538-3011** for the free 15-minute call — ask about the next Foundations class start date and where it meets.
2. **Email Nancy@Intunedogtraining.com** — lead with the weekend-availability question.
3. **Email DogTraining@hssv.org** if budget is the binding constraint — ask about the adopter discount.
4. **Start Week 0 this weekend regardless of who you book.** Every week you wait is another week of him rehearsing the barking.

subtasks.title: Decide: hire a trainer vs. DIY for leash pulling + dog reactivity
subtasks.description:
RECOMMENDATION: Hybrid, weighted toward DIY. Do the daily work yourself, but buy a small amount of professional help up front — specifically the D For Dogz Leash Reactive Foundations group class ($595, Saturdays) or 2–3 private sessions. Do not buy a $2,400+ package yet.

WHY DIY IS VIABLE HERE:
- The daily reps are the treatment. Reactivity work is desensitisation + counter-conditioning done in short sessions on real walks. No trainer can do that for you; you're the one on the other end of the leash every evening. Day-training packages where the trainer works the dog are the worst value for this specific problem.
- Mild-to-moderate reactivity is widely considered manageable by a committed owner. The professional-help thresholds are: a bite history, escaping the harness, or redirected aggression (biting the handler when frustrated). Your description — barks at every dog, pulls hard — reads as garden-variety leash reactivity, not any of those.
- Both problems have well-documented, free protocols: Engage-Disengage / "Look At That" for the reactivity, and stop-when-tight plus reinforce-at-your-side for the pulling.
- Cost of DIY equipment is roughly $95–$165 all in.

WHY BUY SOME HELP ANYWAY:
- 14 months is peak adolescence. Reactivity that shows up now is common and hormone/maturation-linked, and it entrenches with every rehearsal. Getting it right in the first few weeks matters more than usual.
- You need a correct read on WHY he barks, and this changes the plan: FEAR-based reactivity is distance-increasing — he feels trapped by the leash and is trying to make the dog go away. FRUSTRATION-based (barrier) reactivity is the opposite — he desperately wants to greet and can't, and the leash blocks him. A border collie mix that pulls hard toward dogs is often frustration, but treating a fearful dog as frustrated (or vice versa) sends you down the wrong road for weeks. One session with a good trainer settles this.
- A reactive-dog group class also gives you what you cannot manufacture alone: a supply of controlled, predictable trigger dogs at a distance you choose. On a public street you get no say over how close the other dog comes.
- Border collie mix = high drive, high intelligence. The two are also more likely than average to need a real mental-exercise outlet alongside the training.

HARD RULES ON WHO TO HIRE:
- Force-free / positive-reinforcement only. Look for CPDT-KA, KPA-CTP, CBCC-KA, IAABC, or Academy for Dog Trainers (CTC) credentials.
- Avoid board-and-train and any program using e-collars or prong collars for reactivity. These suppress the outward behaviour without changing the underlying emotion, and can make things more dangerous.

BUDGET-DEPENDENT CALL: If money is tight, HSSV group manners is $200/6 weeks and there's an adopter discount — but confirm first that they'll take a reactive dog, and be aware they offer no private consults.

subtasks.title: Write the 4-week week-by-week training plan
subtasks.description:
DONE — the plan is written out as the five child tasks below (Week 0 through Week 4), each with the full detail for that week. Work through them in order.

The plan runs two tracks in parallel every week:
1. LOOSE-LEASH WALKING — short 5-10 min sessions, 5-6 evenings/week, in boring environments first.
2. REACTIVITY — the Engage-Disengage / "Look At That" protocol, 2-4 sessions/week of 1-5 minutes each, always under threshold.
Plus a third supporting track: 2-3 long-line decompression sniffing walks per week, which is not optional for a border collie mix.

The single governing rule across all four weeks: never work closer than the distance at which he can still notice a dog without barking. If he won't take a treat, he's over threshold and you're too close.

Status is `waiting` because these are all human-executed weeks, not agent work.

subtasks.title: Week 0 (this weekend): buy kit and set the walking rules
subtasks.description:
BEFORE week 1 starts. Total spend ~$95-$165.

BUY:
- Front-clip (front-attachment) harness, correctly fitted. This is the single biggest immediate change for a hard puller. Not a prong, not a choke, not an e-collar.
- 6ft fixed-length leash for street walking. No retractable.
- 15-30ft long line for decompression walks in open space.
- Treat pouch that clips to your waist and opens one-handed.
- High-value soft smelly treats he does NOT get otherwise: string cheese, chicken breast, turkey hotdog cut small. Kibble will not cut it near triggers.
- Optional: a clicker. A consistent verbal marker ("yes!") works fine if you'd rather not juggle one more object.

SET THE RULES (this is the management half, and it matters as much as the training):
- For the next 4 weeks, no walk goes anywhere you can't create distance. Avoid narrow sidewalks, avoid the dog park entirely, avoid busy trail times.
- Scout two routes: one QUIET route (wide streets, few dogs, escape options, e.g. an industrial street or a school field in the evening) and one PREDICTABLE route where dogs appear at a distance you control.
- Learn the emergency U-turn before you need it: say a cue word, turn, and toss treats on the ground as you both walk away.
- Rule for the whole 4 weeks: every reactive outburst is a rehearsal that makes it stickier. Your job is to prevent them, not to correct them.

subtasks.title: Week 1: find his threshold distance and reward the loose leash — no trigger work yet
subtasks.description:
GOAL FOR THE WEEK: establish a baseline. You are gathering data and paying for good behaviour. You are not yet trying to fix anything.

LEASH PULLING (5-10 min, 5-6 evenings):
- Do this in the driveway, garage, or an empty quiet street. Not on a real walk.
- Method: walk forward. The instant the leash goes tight, STOP dead. Stand still. The moment there is slack or he glances back at you, mark ("yes") and feed the treat AT YOUR LEG on the side you want him to walk on. Then move forward again. Forward motion is the reward for slack; stopping is the consequence of tight.
- Separately, feed him at your side, at your knee height, every 3-5 steps for no reason at all while the leash is loose. You are building a habit of him wanting to be in that spot.
- Expect this to be slow and boring in week 1. That is correct.

REACTIVITY (2-3 sessions, 5-10 min):
- Park somewhere you can see dogs pass at a long distance — the far edge of a park, your car with the boot open, a bench 100+ feet off a path.
- Do NOTHING but watch and take notes. At what distance does he first notice a dog? At what distance does he stiffen or stare? At what distance does he bark? That barking distance minus a comfortable margin is his THRESHOLD. For most leash-reactive dogs the starting working distance is 50-100 feet.
- Write the number down. Every session for the next three weeks happens further away than that number.

DECOMPRESSION (2-3 times, 30-45 min, weekend friendly):
- Long line in a big open low-dog space. Let him sniff wherever he wants. No training, no commands. A border collie mix on a stressful daily walk is running a permanently elevated baseline; sniffing walks bring it down and make the training sessions work better.

END-OF-WEEK SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE: you know his threshold number, and he can do 10 loose-leash steps in a boring environment.

subtasks.title: Week 2: start Engage-Disengage at threshold distance (Level 1 only)
subtasks.description:
GOAL FOR THE WEEK: change how he FEELS about seeing a dog. Level 1 only — do not rush to Level 2.

ENGAGE-DISENGAGE, LEVEL 1 (3-4 sessions, 1-5 minutes each, then stop):
1. Set up at or beyond the threshold distance you measured in week 1. Be quiet and still. Let him notice the dog on his own — do not point it out, do not say his name.
2. The exact moment he LOOKS at the other dog, mark (click or "yes").
3. When he turns his head back to you after the marker, feed. 
4. If he reacts, or doesn't turn back to you after the marker, you are too close. Move further away and reset. That's information, not failure.

THE BAR TO CLEAR: 3-5 successful reps in a row at the same distance, where a success = he turns back to you immediately after the marker. Only after that do you consider Level 2 (week 3).

IMPORTANT: if the trigger dog is moving, or getting closer, or changing intensity, stay on Level 1 at that distance. Do not advance.

SESSION LENGTH: 1-5 minutes, then a real break. Multiple short sessions beat one long one. Watch for lip-licking, yawning, scratching — those are stress signals, and they mean stop.

LEASH PULLING (continues, 5-10 min, 5-6 evenings):
- Same stop-when-tight rule, but now graduate it to your quiet route with mild distractions.
- Add a name-response game: say his name, mark the head turn, feed. 10 reps. You are buying yourself an emergency handle for week 3.

DECOMPRESSION: 2-3 long-line sniffing walks, unchanged.

END-OF-WEEK SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE: he can see a dog at threshold distance and check back in with you 3-5 times in a row without barking.

subtasks.title: Week 3: move to Level 2 (disengage) and start closing distance in small steps
subtasks.description:
GOAL FOR THE WEEK: he starts choosing to look away from dogs by himself, and you shrink the working distance.

ENGAGE-DISENGAGE, LEVEL 2 (3-4 sessions, 1-5 min each):
1. Let him notice the dog, then WAIT 1-5 seconds. You are waiting for him to look away on his own.
2. The instant he DISENGAGES — looks away from the dog on his own — mark, then feed.
3. If he fixates for more than 5 seconds, drop straight back to Level 1. Fixating is the last quiet moment before a bark.

HOW TO CLOSE DISTANCE: after 3-5 successful Level 2 reps in a row, move 1-5 STEPS closer. That is the entire increment. Not ten feet, not across the road. If the trigger dog is moving or the intensity changes at the new distance, go back to Level 1 there before trying Level 2 again.

EXPECT A BAD DAY. Progress is not linear. One barking episode is not a reset; three sessions in a row that go badly means you moved too fast, so go back to the last distance that worked and stay there a week.

LEASH PULLING (5-10 min, 5-6 evenings):
- Take loose-leash work onto the real quiet route. Reduce the treat rate — instead of every 3-5 steps, go to every 8-10, then intermittently.
- Practise the emergency U-turn 3-4 times per walk when there is NO dog around, so it's automatic when there is.

DECOMPRESSION: maintain 2-3 sniffing walks. If he's coping well, add a short mental-work session indoors — snuffle mat, scatter feed, a puzzle toy. A border collie mix needs a job; an under-stimulated one is a more reactive one.

END-OF-WEEK SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE: he offers a look-away by himself, and your working distance is meaningfully shorter than the week-1 number.

subtasks.title: Week 4: generalise to real walks, then honestly assess whether to escalate
subtasks.description:
GOAL FOR THE WEEK: take it off the training field and onto actual walks, then decide what happens next.

GENERALISE (this is where most people lose the gains):
- Run the same Engage-Disengage game in 3-4 DIFFERENT locations. Dogs learn in context; skills that work at your usual spot often collapse somewhere new. Expect performance to drop in a new place and give yourself extra distance there.
- Vary the trigger: big dogs, small dogs, dogs moving toward you, dogs behind fences.
- On ordinary walks, your default when a dog appears is now: spot it early → get distance or U-turn → play the game if you're under threshold, leave if you're not.

LEASH PULLING:
- Loose leash on the real route with normal distractions. Keep treats on you permanently — reinforcement never fully stops, it just gets thinner.

DO A HONEST 4-WEEK REVIEW. Write down:
- Week-1 threshold distance vs. today's working distance. Is the number smaller?
- How many full reactive outbursts this week vs. week 1?
- Can he take a treat when he sees a dog at working distance? (If he won't eat, he's over threshold — that's your single best real-time gauge.)

ESCALATE TO A PROFESSIONAL IF ANY OF THESE ARE TRUE:
- The threshold distance has not shrunk at all in 4 weeks.
- He is worse, not better.
- You've seen redirected aggression — snapping or biting at you or the leash when frustrated.
- He has escaped or backed out of the harness.
- You dread walks, or you're avoiding them. Handler burnout is a legitimate reason to buy help.

IF IT'S WORKING: keep going. Realistic timeline for meaningful change in leash reactivity is months, not weeks. Four good weeks means the method is right, not that you're finished. Also set a realistic end goal — the target is a dog who can walk calmly past other dogs, not necessarily a dog who plays at the dog park. Plenty of dogs never want that and don't need to.

subtasks.title: Book the free 15-min discovery call with D For Dogz
subtasks.description:
CALL 650-538-3011 (Mon-Fri 9am-7pm, Sat 9am-3pm) or book the free 15-minute call online at dfordogtraining.com. Ask for KT.

ASK THESE FOUR THINGS:
1. When does the next Leash Reactive Dog Foundations class start? ($595, 9 sessions over 5 weeks, Saturdays 9:30-10:30am in person + Wednesdays 6:30-7:15pm on Zoom.)
2. WHERE do the in-person Saturday sessions physically meet? They rotate locations around town - confirm they're drivable for you.
3. Is a 14-month rescue border collie mix who barks at every dog on walks a fit for this class, or would they start with a private session? No bite history toward humans required, vaccinations must be current.
4. In their read, does he sound fear-based or frustration-based? Getting this diagnosis right shapes everything else.

This is the recommended first spend. It's the cheapest way to get controlled, predictable trigger dogs at a distance you control - which you cannot manufacture on a public street.

subtasks.title: Email Nancy at In Tune Dog Training to check weekend availability and tiered pricing
subtasks.description:
EMAIL: Nancy@Intunedogtraining.com (no phone published). Website: intunedogtraining.com

This is your private in-home option, and the cheaper of the two private routes. Pricing: initial consultation $195-$325 (that's two 60-min sessions), follow-ups $130-$215 each. She recommends 6 sessions total, about twice a month.

ASK:
1. Can she do weekend appointments? Her site says weekends "may be available upon request" - it is not guaranteed, so this is the deciding question.
2. Confirm you're inside her service area: 15-mile radius of the Cambrian neighbourhood in San Jose (covers Campbell, Sunnyvale, Cupertino, Santa Clara, Mountain View, Los Gatos, Milpitas, Los Altos).
3. If your household earns under $115K/yr, ask about tiered pricing - see intunedogtraining.com/booktier.
4. Ask where in the $195-$325 / $130-$215 ranges a leash-reactivity case like yours lands.

Do this in parallel with the D For Dogz call so you can compare before committing to either.

subtasks.title: Email HSSV about the adopter discount and whether they'll take a reactive dog
subtasks.description:
EMAIL: DogTraining@hssv.org (Humane Society Silicon Valley, Milpitas)

This is the budget fallback: $200 for a six-session Beginning Manners class, and ADOPTERS GET A DISCOUNT - worth asking about since he's a rescue. You'll need your adoption paperwork / the shelter you adopted from.

ASK:
1. Is a 14-month reactive dog appropriate for Beginning Manners? Their site explicitly asks you to email and describe the specific behaviours first. Describe the barking/lunging at other dogs honestly.
2. What's the adopter discount code / do you qualify?
3. What days and times does the next Beginning Manners class run? Multi-session classes run the same weekday and time each week for six weeks, so you need one repeatable slot.

NOTE: HSSV does NOT offer private training or behaviour consults to the general public. If they say he's not suited to a group class, they'll only give you a referral - so treat this as the cheap option, not the reactivity-specialist option.

FREE ANYWAY: download their Reactive Dog Training Guide PDF from hssv.org/services/dog-services/training/ - costs nothing and is worth reading before week 1.

subtasks.title: Decide which option to book, then start Week 0
subtasks.description:
Once the D For Dogz call and Nancy's email reply are in, pick one and book it. Decision shortcut:

- Want structured practice around real trigger dogs, and Saturday mornings work -> D For Dogz Leash Reactive Foundations, $595.
- Want someone in your actual neighbourhood on your actual walking route, and weekends check out -> In Tune, ~$845-$1,400 for a 6-session block, less with tiered pricing.
- Money is the binding constraint -> HSSV $200 (if they'll take him) plus do the DIY plan properly.
- DON'T buy the $2,400 D For Dogz private coaching or the $4,200 day-training yet. Neither is justified before you've seen how he responds to four weeks of consistent work.

Whichever you pick, START WEEK 0 THIS WEEKEND regardless. The kit and the route-scouting are worth doing before any trainer's first session, and every week you wait is another week of him rehearsing the barking.
